concept_note.title: Python Basics: Intermediate
concept_note.summary: Building on variables and arithmetic, this lesson introduces functions, loops, and lists — the three Python constructs that appear in every AI training loop.
learning_goals: Write reusable functions with def and return
Iterate over sequences with for loops
Store collections of values with lists
Read a small gradient descent loop in Python
concept_note.long_intro: You already know variables and arithmetic. Now it is time for the three constructs that turn small scripts into real programs: functions (reusable blocks of logic), for loops (repeating an action over a collection), and lists (holding many values in one variable). Every training loop you will ever read uses all three. The training loop takes a list of data points, iterates over them with a for loop, and calls a function to compute the loss and update the weights. Once you can read these three constructs, you can read most of the code in an intro AI course.

deep_explanation.heading: Functions: naming a computation
deep_explanation.body: A function is a named block of code that takes some inputs (arguments) and produces an output (the return value). You define one with def name(args): and you call it later with name(values). Functions are how you avoid writing the same logic over and over. In AI code, functions are everywhere: a loss function, a forward pass function, an optimizer step function. The point of a function is that once you have named the computation, you can call it wherever you need it — and you can test it in isolation.
deep_explanation.code:
def double(x):
    return x * 2

result = double(5)
print(result)   # shows 10

deep_explanation.heading: For loops: doing something many times
deep_explanation.body: A for loop runs a block of code once for each item in a sequence. The Python syntax is 'for item in sequence:'. On every iteration, the variable 'item' holds the next value from the sequence. This is how training loops iterate over data, how layers iterate over neurons, and how evaluation loops iterate over test examples. If you see 'for step in range(100):' in a tutorial, it means the code inside will run 100 times.

deep_explanation.heading: Lists: holding many values
deep_explanation.body: A list is an ordered collection of values. You write it with square brackets: [1, 2, 3] or ['a', 'b', 'c']. You can add to it with .append(), read the i-th element with list[i], and get the length with len(list). Lists are how you store a batch of training examples, the weights of a model, or the losses from each step. Everywhere you need to hold many values under one name, you use a list.
deep_explanation.code:
losses = []
for step in range(5):
    loss = 10 - step
    losses.append(loss)
print(losses)   # shows [10, 9, 8, 7, 6]

deep_explanation.heading: Putting it together: a mini training loop
deep_explanation.body: Here is a tiny version of what a real training loop looks like. It has all the pieces you have learned: a function that computes something, a for loop that repeats, and a list that collects results. Real training loops are the same shape, just with more math inside the function and millions of iterations instead of five. When you read AI code, look for this shape and the rest becomes readable.
deep_explanation.code:
def compute_loss(x):
    return (x - 3) ** 2

x = 0.0
learning_rate = 0.1
losses = []

for step in range(10):
    loss = compute_loss(x)
    losses.append(loss)
    gradient = 2 * (x - 3)
    x = x - learning_rate * gradient

print("final x:", x)

concept_note.formal_definition: A function is defined with def name(params): and returns a value with return. A for loop iterates over any iterable (list, range, string, etc.) and binds each element to a loop variable. A list is a mutable ordered sequence, created with [items] or list(), extended with .append(), indexed with [i], and measured with len().

code_example.universal_explanation: The function takes a list of numbers, adds them one by one in a loop, and divides by the length to get the average. This same pattern appears inside every evaluation script in AI: iterate over results, sum them, divide by the count.

common_mistakes: Forgetting to return a value from a function: without return, the function produces None, and the caller gets nothing back.
Reusing the same variable name inside and outside a function without realizing they are different scopes: the a inside the function is not the same as the a outside it.
Off-by-one errors in range: range(5) produces 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 — it does not include 5. This trips up beginners constantly.
Mutating a list while iterating over it: adding or removing items during a for loop produces surprising behavior. Iterate over a copy or collect changes separately.
Calling a function before defining it: Python reads top to bottom, so the def must come before the call.
concept_note.real_world_usage: This is the exact shape of every training loop in AI. PyTorch's classic example loop reads: 'for epoch in range(num_epochs): for batch in dataloader: loss = compute_loss(model(batch)); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()'. That is a for loop iterating over a list (the dataloader), calling functions (model and compute_loss), and collecting results. Once you can read our mini version, you can read the real one.
key_takeaways: Functions package logic under a name so it can be reused.
For loops repeat a block for each item in a sequence.
Lists hold many values under one name.
Every AI training loop is a for loop over a list calling functions.
